_comment: THE ONE STATEMENT OF HOW THIS SITE WRITES A EURO AMOUNT.
Read by sources/number_format.py and by web/lib/money.ts. Not mirrored — read.
Two copies of a rule is one rule that will eventually disagree with itself, and this
file exists because that had already happened: build_opportunity.py rendered a total
with Python's format spec, web/lib/transition.ts rendered the same total with
toFixed, and the two round a tie in opposite directions. Steel committed exactly
€3,250,000,000 and the sector page printed '€3.2 billion' and '€3.3 bn' four lines
apart. Cement's €421 million could not tell them apart, so it shipped invisible.
WHAT IS SHARED AND WHAT IS NOT. The NUMBER is shared and must be identical on both
sides: which tier it falls in, how many decimals it keeps, and how it rounds. The
UNIT WORD is not: prose says 'billion' because a sentence has room for it, a table
cell says 'bn' because it does not. Both words are declared here so the difference
is a decision rather than an accident.
ROUNDING IS HALF AWAY FROM ZERO, and it is applied to the number's shortest
round-trip DECIMAL representation rather than to a binary scaling of it. Both
languages produce that representation identically — Python's repr(), JavaScript's
String() — and both implementations round its digits. Scaling in binary first is
what makes 1.005 × 100 come out as 100.49999999999999 and round down in one
language and up in the other; rounding the digits cannot do that.
`cases` IS THE GATE. A declaration that both sides round half away from zero proves
nothing about whether both sides DO. These vectors are the behaviour, they include
every tie and every tier boundary, and both implementations are checked against
them: sources/check_number_format.py on the Python side, web/lib/money.test.mts on
the TypeScript side, which the prebuild chain already runs.
TWO SHAPES OF FIGURE, AND THEY ARE NOT THE SAME RULE. An AMOUNT is a stock — money
committed, money awarded — and is written at the scale that suits its size, so it
takes the tiers below. A RATE is a price per unit, always quoted at the same
precision because that is how the thing is traded, so it takes `rate` and no tiers:
a carbon cost of €75.46 per tonne does not become '€75 per tonne' because it is
small, and it does not become '€0.0 million per tonne' because the tiers exist.
`rate` is implemented in Python only, because nothing in TypeScript formats one —
rates are built into the stored strings and rendered as they are. It is stated here
rather than in the Python module so that the day TypeScript needs one, the rule is
already written and there is nothing to invent.
THREE FORMS, BECAUSE THERE ARE THREE SPACE BUDGETS. Prose has room for 'billion';
a table cell has room for 'bn'; a diagram node is 236 units wide and has room for
neither the space nor the word, so it takes 'm' welded to the figure. The three are
declared together here so that a surface picks one rather than inventing a fourth,
which is what the diagram had done.
